strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: whether recurrent memory mechanisms from NLP (e.g., RMT) can extend the effective context of sequence-modeling RL agents beyond the ~30-frame saturation point reported for Decision Transformer.

The RMDT architecture and training procedure (segment-wise teacher forcing, memory passing with gradient detachment, segment overlap and memory fixation for MuJoCo) are described in reasonable detail, with useful figures.
A dedicated DT-XL baseline (same segmentation, no memory tokens) is included, which allows some isolation of the contribution of memory tokens rather than just longer contexts.

A systematic ablation study on number of segments, memory size, segment overlay, and memory fixation, plus qualitative attention-map analyses (Sections 6-7 and Appendix B) that provide some interpretability evidence.
Code and model weights are stated to be publicly available, and hyperparameters are listed in Appendix A.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a straightforward application of the existing Recurrent Memory Transformer (Bulatov et al., 2022) to the Decision Transformer framework. The conceptual contribution is an engineering combination rather than a new memory or offline RL technique.

The central claim of significant superiority is not well supported. On MuJoCo, RMDT's mean normalized score (75.2) is below CQL (77.6) and roughly equal to DT and TAP (74.7), with several environments clearly worse than DT (e.g., Medium-Expert Walker2d 84.7 vs 108.1; Medium-Replay HalfCheetah 35.9 vs 36.6). The conclusion's statement that the model 'significantly outperforms ... TAP' is inconsistent with Table 2.

Very narrow benchmark coverage: only 4 of ~40+ Atari games, explicitly due to 'limited computation resources', and only 3 locomotion environments. The strong environment-dependence of the results (e.g., only Medium Hopper improves markedly) makes general claims about memory in offline RL premature.

Evaluation rigor is weak: only 3 seeds and 10 episodes per seed, no statistical significance tests, and several Atari comparisons (e.g., Breakout 123.8±35.6 vs 99.6±29.8; Pong 17.1±0.94 vs 16.6±0.99) have heavily overlapping confidence intervals. Raw (non-normalized) Atari scores also complicate cross-paper comparison.

Hyperparameter and ablation protocol concerns: MuJoCo-specific choices (25% segment overlap, memory fixation) appear to be selected via evaluation on the same environments reported in Table 2, raising tuning-on-test concerns; the paper does not clarify whether hyperparameters were chosen on held-out settings.

No computational cost analysis. The paper motivates the work by the quadratic complexity of transformers, but does not report wall-clock time, memory footprint, or the added overhead of memory tokens and multi-segment training relative to DT/DT-XL, so the claimed efficiency benefits are not quantified.

Missing comparisons to closely related long-context RL baselines (e.g., Gato-style long-context transformers, Online Decision Transformer with longer contexts, or other memory-augmented approaches like Compressive Transformer applied to RL), limiting the ability to attribute gains specifically to recurrent memory.

Presentation issues: the repository link appears as a placeholder/empty string in both the abstract and Appendix; references [8]/[9] are duplicates; the main results table (Table 1) mixes normalized and raw conventions without clarity for readers; MuJoCo training description (segment start contexts 'starting from zero') is under-specified.

Scalability claims for 'real-world applications' and longer contexts are speculative, as experiments saturate at only 3 segments / 150 frames, which is still a short horizon; evidence for memory actually enabling longer-horizon tasks is not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question: whether recurrent memory mechanisms can extend the effective context length of Decision Transformer–style models in offline RL.

The proposed RMDT combines established components (RMT memory tokens, Transformer-XL-style segment recurrence) in a reasonable and clearly described architecture, with training/evaluation procedures illustrated (Figures 2–4).

The paper includes several ablations (number of segments, memory size, memory-token removal, segment overlay/memory fixation) and a qualitative attention-map analysis supporting that memory tokens are actually used.
Code and model weights are stated to be publicly available, and hyperparameters are listed in the appendix, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the contribution is essentially porting existing RMT memory tokens [31] into the Decision Transformer framework [23]. No new memory mechanism or theoretical insight is introduced, and the technical machinery is directly borrowed from prior work.

Weak and incomplete evaluation: only 4 Atari games are used (explicitly due to 'limited computation resources'), out of the dozens in the DQN replay benchmark, so the Atari results may not generalize. Only 3 seeds with 10 episodes each are used, with no statistical significance testing; several gains (e.g., Pong 17.1±0.94 vs 16.6±0.99) are within noise, making the claim of being 'significantly superior' unsupported.

Mixed and unconvincing MuJoCo results: RMDT underperforms CQL and TAP on Medium-Replay (all three tasks) and performs poorly on Medium-Expert Walker2d (84.7 vs 108.8 for CQL); the mean score (75.2) is only marginally above DT/TAP (74.7) and below CQL (77.6). The headline claim of superiority is contradicted by Table 2.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and possibly unfair: DT baselines were rerun by the authors rather than cited, no comparison to other long-context or memory-augmented RL methods (e.g., GTrXL, Online DT, or other memory-augmented policies), and TAP/CQL numbers are taken from a third-party paper.

The claimed context-extension benefit is modest: performance saturates at ~5 segments (~90–150 frames) and even degrades on Seaquest, while the paper motivates memory for very long contexts that are never actually demonstrated.
The 'memory survey' (Section 7) is purely qualitative attention-map analysis on single, randomly selected examples; no quantitative probing of what information memory tokens retain is provided.

Significant tuning asymmetry: the final MuJoCo pipeline (25% segment overlay + memory fixation) was selected based on ablations, but the effect of this selection on the headline comparison is not clearly disentangled, and Atari results show no dependence on these choices, weakening the generality of the design.

Presentation and rigor issues: duplicated reference [8]=[9], a garbled Equation (1), empty repository link ('publicly available in repository'), typos ('MoJoko'), and inconsistent numbering/formatting of dataset settings suggest insufficient polishing.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: extending the effective context length of Decision Transformer-style offline RL agents, which is a known limitation of the original DT (saturating at ~30 frames).

The proposed RMDT is a clean and clearly described combination of the Recurrent Memory Transformer mechanism with the Decision Transformer framework, including a well-motivated training procedure (segment-wise teacher forcing with detached memory passing, segment overlays, memory fixation).

The paper includes a useful controlled baseline (DT-XL) that isolates the contribution of memory tokens from simply concatenating more context, and the Atari results show a consistent improvement with reduced variance.

The ablation study is reasonably thorough: number of segments, memory size, segment overlay, and memory fixation are all examined, and the paper reports which configuration is used for the main results.

The attention-map analysis (main text and Appendix B) provides qualitative evidence that memory tokens are actually read from and written to in a structured way, supporting the claim that memory is being used rather than ignored.
The code and model weights are stated to be publicly released, and hyperparameters are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the paper is essentially a straightforward integration of the existing RMT memory-token mechanism [31] into the existing Decision Transformer [23]. There is no new algorithmic insight, theoretical analysis, or fundamentally new technique; the contribution is an application of a known NLP memory mechanism to a known RL sequence-modeling framework.

The evaluation scope is narrow: only 4 Atari games (due to 'limited computation resources') and 3 MuJoCo environments. Given that Atari results vary substantially across games, 4 environments with 3 seeds each is insufficient to support the claim of 'significant superiority' — no statistical significance tests are reported.

The MuJoCo results are mixed and do not support the headline claims. RMDT's mean normalized score (75.2) is essentially identical to DT (74.7) and TAP (74.7) and below CQL (77.6). Several individual results are clearly worse (e.g., Walker2d Medium-Expert: 84.7 vs. TAP's 107.4 and CQL's 108.8; all Medium-Replay results are below CQL). Yet the conclusion claims the model 'significantly outperforms... TAP', which the presented evidence does not support — this is an overclaim.
The variance of the RMDT results on MuJoCo is high (e.g., ±14.4, ±18.9), and with only 3 seeds it is unclear whether improvements such as Hopper Medium (84.6 vs. 67.6) are robust.

Atari results are reported only as raw scores without the normalized protocol used in the DT paper, making direct comparison with published numbers harder; and only a small subset of games is covered.

Some design decisions are under-justified: e.g., memory tokens at both sequence ends, the specific gradient-detachment scheme, and the choice of 15 memory tokens receive only empirical, environment-limited justification. The paper itself admits the benefit saturates at ~3 segments and that memory size does not matter, which weakens the practical significance of the memory mechanism in these benchmarks.

There are presentation and citation quality issues: 'MoJoko' typos, duplicated references ([8] and [9] are the same Transformer-XL paper), an apparently incorrect citation ([22], Deformable DETR, cited for RMT's 1M-token context), and an incomplete repository URL in the abstract and page 12.

The claimed motivation (long-context needs in robotics/self-driving) is not actually tested — all experiments use short-horizon Atari/MuJoCo tasks where the paper's own ablations show context saturation, so the practical value proposition remains unvalidated.

Related work on long-context sequence modeling for RL (e.g., other efficient/context-extended decision transformers) could be discussed and compared more explicitly; only DT-XL is compared as a context-extension baseline.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated limitation of Decision Transformer-style offline RL: fixed context length and quadratic attention cost, which prevents capturing long-term dependencies. Applying recurrent memory tokens (inspired by RMT) to offline RL sequence models is a sensible and reasonably novel contribution.

Evaluation covers a good breadth of settings: two purpose-built memory-intensive environments (VizDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze) plus standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, demonstrating the model is competitive even where memory is not required.

The proposed training procedures (segment-wise training, curriculum learning for memory-dependent tasks, starting trajectories from the beginning) are clearly described and the necessity of these modifications is justified.

Thorough ablations: effect of number of segments, memory token count, memory token replacement with noise, curriculum vs. no curriculum, and attention-map interpretability analysis providing qualitative evidence that memory tokens are actually used.
Source code is publicly released, aiding reproducibility; a limitation section is included and honest about applicability to short sequences.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the architecture is essentially RMT memory tokens grafted onto Decision Transformer. The main new elements are training-procedure engineering (curriculum, segment-wise training). The claim of being 'the first attempt to adapt transformers with memory to RL' is overstated given prior work such as TrMRL, AdA (Transformer-XL memory), and GTrXL.

A key missing baseline: DT equipped with Transformer-XL-style cached hidden states (the standard recurrence mechanism) is not compared against, which is the most natural alternative for extending context; this weakens the case that learned memory tokens specifically are responsible for the gains.

Statistical rigor is limited: only 3 seeds for Atari and MuJoCo, and the headline VizDoom result has very high variance (16.46 ± 6.90 vs. 6.08 ± 1.62), so the significance of the main claim rests on few runs; no significance tests are reported.

Some results and design choices appear ad hoc: the modified T-Maze deviates from the standard benchmark; the 'novel evaluation strategy' for MuJoCo (resetting target return at each segment) changes the standard evaluation protocol without sufficient justification or evidence it is fair; comparison numbers for CQL/TAP/DT are taken from prior papers rather than re-run under identical conditions.

Presentation issues: confusing naming (RATE- vs. RATE in Table 3), typos ('memory toxins', 'interference' for inference), and notation inconsistencies (R_{t+1} defined at time step i+1) reduce clarity.

The memory benefit in MuJoCo is admitted to be minimal, and Atari gains over DT are attributed post-hoc to vague 'intricate dynamics' rather than demonstrated; the practical impact of the method on standard benchmarks is therefore modest, and the main value is confined to memory-intensive toy settings.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: extending sequence-modeled offline RL (Decision Transformer) to memory-intensive environments is a relevant direction.

Thorough ablation studies: the paper investigates number of segments, memory size, and the role of memory tokens via inference-time interventions (noise replacement, fixed memory), which lends credibility to the claim that memory is actually used.
Attention-map analysis of read/write memory tokens provides a nice interpretability angle.
Results on VizDoom-Two-Colors and T-Maze convincingly show that DT without memory cannot retain information beyond its context window, while RATE does.
Code is publicly released, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially the Recurrent Memory Transformer (Bulatov et al., 2022) applied to Decision Transformer. The claim of being 'the first attempt to adapt transformer models with memory to generate agent actions' is overstated, given prior work such as Gated Transformer-XL, TrMRL, AdA, and Working Memory Graphs in RL settings.

The core evaluation is confounded by non-standard modifications: (a) the T-Maze environment is modified from the standard benchmark (Ni et al., 2023), so results are not comparable with prior memory-RL literature; (b) for MuJoCo, the authors introduce a 'novel evaluation strategy' where each segment starts with the maximum return. This changes the conditioning protocol relative to DT/TAP/CQL, making the direct comparisons in Table 4 questionable.

Atari evaluation covers only 4 games and the Q*bert result (13518 for RATE vs. 2215 for DT) is an enormous discrepancy that goes largely unexplained and is not corroborated by normalized scores or a standard evaluation protocol; claims of general superiority over DT rest on very thin evidence.

Statistical rigor is limited: 3 seeds for Atari/MuJoCo, and the ViZDoom-Two-Colors results have very high variance (RATE 16.46±6.90 vs. DT90 6.08±1.62), so the headline claim of significant improvement needs stronger support.

On MuJoCo Medium-Replay (arguably the hardest and most informative setting), RATE underperforms both DT and CQL on Hopper, and the overall gains over DT are marginal; the paper's own analysis concedes memory contributes minimally in these tasks, which weakens the 'better or comparable results' claim.

The training procedure differs from DT in multiple ways simultaneously (starting trajectories from the beginning, curriculum learning, segment-wise sampling, modified return conditioning), so improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to the memory mechanism rather than the training changes; the RATE- ablation partially addresses this but not for the curriculum and return-conditioning confounds.
Writing and presentation issues: inconsistent notation (R_{t+1} defined with index i+1), typos ('memory toxins', 'inferense'), and the appendix references a repository URL that appears incomplete.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and important limitation of Decision Transformer-style models: the quadratic cost of attention restricts usable context, which matters in memory-dependent environments. Extending RMT-style memory tokens to offline RL is a sensible and well-motivated direction.

The evaluation covers both memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, a modified T-Maze) and standard benchmarks (Atari DQN replay, D4RL MuJoCo), which supports the claim that memory does not hurt performance when it is not needed.

The memory-specific training procedure (sequential segment processing with detached-but-propagating memory, curriculum learning for T-Maze) is clearly described and addresses a real problem (sparse, episode-start-dependent signals) rather than simply applying RMT off the shelf.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: number of segments, memory size, memory token removal (RATE-), memory token replacement with noise/first-segment tokens, and curriculum-vs-no-curriculum comparisons.

Interpretability analysis via attention maps (read/write memory patterns) provides qualitative evidence that memory tokens are actually used, and the code is publicly available, supporting reproducibility.

On T-Maze, the comparison is convincing: DT degrades to ~50% success beyond its context length while RATE maintains 100% up to 3K and degrades more slowly, and DT-9 could not even be trained due to memory limits, illustrating the practical advantage.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core mechanism is essentially the RMT memory token scheme (Bulatov et al., 2022) applied to Decision Transformer trajectories. The related-work claim of being 'the first attempt' is overstated given prior work on memory/recurrence in RL transformers (GTrXL, TrMRL, AdA/Transformer-XL memory).

Baseline coverage is thin. The main memory-task comparisons are only against DT (and the internal RATE- ablation); no comparison against recurrent baselines (LSTM/GTrXL-style policies), online memory-augmented agents, or other long-context approaches. CQL/TAP numbers on MuJoCo are copied from other papers, and RATE underperforms CQL/TAP on several Medium/Medium-Replay settings.

Statistical support is modest: three seeds for Atari/MuJoCo, and ViZDoom-Two-Colors results have very large variance (16.46 ± 6.90 vs. 7.40 ± 1.52), which weakens the headline claim of 'significant' improvement; no significance tests are reported.

Some evidence is internally inconsistent with the memory narrative: replacing memory tokens with first-segment tokens (no updating) yields SR = 100% up to L = 100K on T-Maze, suggesting the updated recurrent memory may be less essential than claimed in at least one environment; this deserves deeper analysis.

The proposed 'novel evaluation strategy' for MuJoCo (restarting each segment at maximum return) modifies the standard DT/RTG conditioning protocol, which complicates direct comparison with published DT/TAP/CQL numbers; the necessity and side effects of this change are not ablated.

The T-Maze environment is a nonstandard modification of the classical T-Maze (extra flag variable, noise channel, four actions), making comparisons to prior memory-RL literature impossible; only four Atari games are evaluated.

Presentation issues: several confusing or contradictory passages (e.g., the memory-token gradient discussion, 'memory toxins' typo, the claim that the same memory embeddings appear at both sequence ends), and the description of training/procedure is spread across Sections 2–4, which hurts clarity.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: extending offline RL sequence models (Decision Transformer style) to long-horizon, memory-intensive POMDPs where information must be used beyond the attention context.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid.Memory) plus standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, with a purpose-built diagnostic environment (Action Associative Retrieval) that provides a relatively explicit test of memory use.

Thoughtful ablations: component-level analysis (memory embeddings vs. cached hidden states vs. MRV), five MRV design variants compared, noise-replacement probe showing information is stored in memory tokens, and curriculum learning analysis.
Favorable computational profile: segment-wise processing reduces GPU memory roughly N-fold relative to DT while keeping parameter count nearly identical, supported by the technical details table.
Demonstrates consistent improvements over DT on MuJoCo (9/9 tasks) and clear out-of-context memory retention in ViZDoom and T-Maze experiments.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the core design is essentially the Recurrent Memory Transformer (Bulatov et al., 2022) applied to the Decision Transformer, with memory embeddings at segment boundaries and hidden-state reuse directly inherited; the MRV is a fairly standard cross-attention/gating combination. The paper would benefit from clearer articulation of what is new beyond adapting RMT to offline RL.

Comparison fairness concerns: RATE is trained with curriculum learning on T-Maze while DT appears not to be, and a non-standard MuJoCo return-conditioning scheme (each segment initialized with maximum return) is introduced for RATE; these asymmetric choices make it hard to attribute gains purely to the memory mechanism.

Standard benchmark evaluation is thin and partly non-comparable: only 4 Atari games are tested, and Atari/Mamba baseline numbers are copied from other papers rather than re-run, with raw (unnormalized) scores that may not follow identical protocols; Memory Maze improvements are modest (1.91 vs 1.45) with wide error bars.

Missing comparisons with relevant memory-augmented RL baselines (e.g., AdA, DT with working memory [28], Transformer-XL-based DT variants) and with an online-memory upper bound; the claim of being 'the first attempt' to adapt memory transformers to offline RL is asserted but not rigorously defended against prior work such as [28].

Writing and presentation issues: repeated grammatical errors ('This proofs that...', 'in thein Table 3', 'oh the pillar'), a likely typo in Eq. 5 (sqrt(h) instead of sqrt(d_k)), unclear notational definitions, and some prose that is hard to follow; the paper reads as a draft in places.

Some claims are under-supported: statements about RATE 'actually using memory' rely on indirect probes; the theoretical condition in Eq. 7 is informal; the argument that SeaQuest vs. Breakout differences stem from memory demand is speculative without targeted analysis.
Statistical rigor is uneven: some experiments use 3 runs only (Atari, Memory Maze), and the high variance in Atari results (e.g., Qbert) weakens the significance of reported gains.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a comprehensive set of appendices detailing environments, training procedures, hyperparameters, and compute.

The evaluation covers a broad range of settings (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid.Memory, Atari, MuJoCo) with multiple seeds, error bars, and a dedicated ablation of five MRV variants.
The proposed Action Associative Retrieval diagnostic and the analysis of whether the agent truly uses memory (Eq. 7, Figure 7) are a nice touch beyond simply reporting rewards.
Technical details such as parameter-count parity with DT and GPU/memory comparisons support a reasonably fair comparison against the Decision Transformer baseline.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core architecture is essentially the Recurrent Memory Transformer [8] (memory tokens passed between segments) plus Transformer-XL-style hidden-state caching applied to Decision Transformer. The Memory Retention Valve is a modest addition (a cross-attention gating on memory updates), and the claim of being 'the first attempt to adapt transformer models with memory to Offline-RL' overlooks closely related work such as DT with internal working memory [28] and online memory-transformer agents (e.g., AdA [4], TWM [10/39]).

Baseline coverage is thin for the central claims. The only baseline actually run in memory-intensive environments is DT; there is no comparison against established memory-capable RL baselines from Ni et al. [35] or online memory models, despite the paper framing itself around POMDP memory problems. DMamba/MambaDM results on Atari/MuJoCo are copied from other papers under potentially different protocols rather than evaluated under a unified setup.

Comparability concerns in the evaluation protocol: (a) the MuJoCo experiments introduce a non-standard return-annotation strategy ('each segment commences with the maximum return'), which makes the comparisons to published DT/CQL/TAP numbers under the standard protocol questionable; (b) RATE uses curriculum learning on T-Maze while it is unclear whether DT received equivalent treatment; (c) the Memory Maze improvement (1.91 vs 1.45) is small in absolute terms, and RATE underperforms on SeaQuest, weakening the 'universality' claim.

The 'long sequence' motivation is oversold. Effective contexts in the main experiments are only 90–150 environment steps (inference up to ~900 in T-Maze), far from the long-context regime (100k+ tokens) that motivates memory transformers; DT with a modestly larger context could plausibly close much of the gap, but this is not tested.

Only 4 Atari games are reported, which is a small subset of the standard 30+ game protocol, and the paper's own explanation for the Atari gains (past actions influencing Breakout/Qbert) is speculative and unverified.

Signs of insufficient polish: the scaling term in Eq. 5 is √h rather than √d_k; typos such as 'This proofs', 'The best results in thein Table 3', 'The best results in their Table 3'; references [57]/[58] are duplicates; the AAR analysis (Figure 7) is described in a way that conflates training/validation observations without clear statistical support.

The claims in the abstract and conclusion ('significantly improve performance', 'better or comparable results against SOTA') are stronger than the evidence: results on standard benchmarks are mixed (losses to DMamba/MambaDM on SeaQuest and several MuJoCo datasets), and the memory-intensive gains are only demonstrated against a memory-less DT baseline.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and relevant problem: extending offline RL sequence models (Decision Transformer) beyond a fixed context to handle POMDP/memory-intensive tasks, which is an underexplored direction relative to online RL.

Experimental coverage is broad: four memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid.Memory), a custom AAR diagnostic environment, plus Atari and MuJoCo, with reasonable numbers of runs and seeds (e.g., 6 runs × 100 seeds on ViZDoom).

The evaluation includes useful analysis beyond headline scores: inference on corridors/mazes much longer than the training context (Figure 5), ablations replacing memory embeddings with noise, a component ablation (memory embeddings, hidden-state caching, MRV), and a well-designed MRV architecture study comparing five variants (Table 3, Figure 8).

The MRV mechanism is motivated by a concrete failure mode (information leaking from memory during intermediate segments) and the empirical results (MRV-CA-2 clearly beating w/o-MRV baseline) support its design.
Practical benefits are quantified: parameter overhead is small (~10^3), and training uses substantially less GPU memory than DT due to segment processing.
The AAR environment and the probability-correlation analysis (Figure 7) provide an explicit test that the model actually uses memory rather than relying on contextual shortcuts.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core design is largely a combination of existing components (RMT memory tokens [8], Transformer-XL-style hidden state caching [16]) applied to the Decision Transformer framework. MRV is essentially a cross-attention memory update, close to mechanisms in Memformer/MART; the paper should more sharply delineate what is architecturally new versus recombined.

The main baseline (DT) has no memory mechanism by construction, so its failure on memory tasks is expected rather than informative. There are no comparisons against memory-capable offline RL baselines (e.g., the internal working-memory DT of Kang et al. [28], or online memory agents adapted to these settings), which weakens the central claims.

The MuJoCo evaluation protocol is modified (each segment starts with the maximum return), and results are presented as RATE outperforming DT in 9/9 cases; however, this nonstandard return construction changes the task definition relative to prior work, making comparisons to reported CQL/DT/TAP/DMamba numbers of unclear fairness. This needs justification and ideally a control experiment.

Atari/MambaDM/DMamba results are taken from other papers rather than re-run under a unified setup, and only 4 Atari games with 3 runs are used; several Atari/MuJoCo gains over Mamba baselines are within one standard deviation (e.g., SeaQuest, HalfCheetah, MR Hopper), so claims of 'better or comparable' results are only partially supported.

T-Maze, the flagship memory result, uses curriculum learning for the headline RATE numbers; while the paper states plain training also works, the exact gap without CL is not cleanly quantified in the main text.

Reproducibility is questionable: no code release is mentioned despite the method having many implementation details (segment handling, memory detach, CL schedule, encoders), and some dataset-construction choices (e.g., ViZDoom trajectories always starting facing the pillar) are environment-specific.

The paper has notable writing/presentation issues (e.g., 'This proofs that', 'results in thein Table 3', unclear notation in Eq. 5 where the softmax scaling is written with sqrt(h)), and the loss/architecture description has ambiguities (Eq. 1 vs Eq. 2 notation is inconsistent).

The claim of being 'the first attempt to adapt transformer models with memory to generate agent actions' in offline RL overstates the gap given prior works like Kang et al. [28] and AdA [4] that the paper itself cites; positioning should be more careful.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory) as well as standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, which is broader than most offline RL papers

Thoughtful analysis experiments: replacing memory tokens/cached states with noise (Figures 6-7), the OracleDT upper-bound construct, and the AAR diagnostic environment provide insight into *where* information is stored (memory embeddings vs. cached hidden states)
The MRV ablation study (Table 6) comparing five alternative memory-update mechanisms (cross-attention variants, gating, GRU, LSTM) is informative and motivates the design choice
Clear identification of the 'information leakage' problem in recurrent memory updating and a well-motivated diagnosis of why DT fails in POMDPs beyond its context
Honest limitations section; hyperparameters and training details are reported in sufficient detail (Tables 8, 9, 11) for approximate reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the model is essentially a combination of existing components — RMT-style memory embeddings (Bulatov et al., 2022), TrXL hidden-state caching (Dai et al., 2019) — applied to the Decision Transformer, with MRV being a fairly small cross-attention gating addition. The core contribution is incremental

A directly relevant memory-augmented DT baseline is missing: Kang et al. (2023) 'Think before you act: Decision transformers with internal working memory' is cited but not compared against, despite being the closest prior work. AMAGO (Grigsby et al., 2024) is also cited but not evaluated

Evaluation fairness concerns: DT is trained with K = K_eff while memory models use K << K_eff over segments; the feed-forward block is disabled only for RATE because it 'works slightly better' (Appendix D); and the MuJoCo evaluation introduces a 'novel evaluation strategy' (resetting return-to-go per segment) that changes the protocol relative to reported baselines — these choices could systematically favor RATE

Improvements on non-memory benchmarks are modest or mixed: Memory Maze (7.64 vs 7.27 for RMT), Atari (loses to MambaDM on 2/4 games), and MuJoCo mean score (78.5) is below MambaDM (79.0) and Mamba-based baselines despite claims of versatility
Several results are within or near reported variance (e.g., Minigrid-Memory interpolates slightly worse than TrXL), weakening the 'consistently outperforms strong baselines' claim
No code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the many environment modifications (altered T-Maze formulation, modified ViZDoom task) on which results depend

Writing quality issues (e.g., 'curing inference', 'Transforer', Figure 3 subpanels hard to parse) and some confusing notation around MRV-CA-1 vs MRV-CA-2 between Algorithm 2 and the ablation descriptions

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem (long-context / POMDP offline RL with transformers) and evaluates on a reasonably broad set of memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory) in addition to standard Atari/MuJoCo benchmarks.

The ablation studies are relatively thorough: component-noise interventions (Figures 6, 7) that probe whether memory is actually used, an OracleDT upper-bound construction (Table 5), a comparison of five MRV variants (Table 6), and additional hyperparameter ablations in the appendix.
The writing is generally clear, and the model is specified in enough detail (Algorithms 1-2, hyperparameter Table 8, training details in Appendix D) to give a reasonable sense of reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the architecture is essentially a combination of existing components - recurrent memory embeddings from RMT (Bulatov et al., 2022), cached hidden states from Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019), applied to the Decision Transformer. The main claimed contribution, the Memory Retention Valve, is a small cross-attention gating block over memory tokens; this is an incremental modification rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, and the paper does not clearly distinguish RATE from simply 'RMT applied to DT'.

Suspicious baseline results undermine the evaluation: the DLSTM, DGRU, and DMamba baselines report SR = 0.5 on T-Maze at T = 90 (Table 1), i.e., at or within the effective context where the clue is trivially available in the input. This strongly suggests the recurrent baselines were under-trained or misconfigured rather than genuinely lacking memory capacity, making the claimed superiority over RNN/SSM baselines unconvincing.

Atari evaluation is narrow (only 4 games: Breakout, Qbert, SeaQuest, Pong), reported in raw rather than normalized scores, making comparison with prior work difficult; the claim of 'better or comparable results to state-of-the-art Mamba-based models' rests on very limited coverage.

The MuJoCo evaluation protocol is modified ('each segment commences with the maximum return') relative to the standard DT protocol; this changes the return-conditioning distribution and makes direct comparisons with published DT/TAP/CQL numbers questionable, and the paper provides no experiment validating that this protocol is fair to the baselines.

Key related baselines are missing: Kang et al. (2023, Decision Transformers with internal working memory) is cited as relevant prior work on memory in DT but never empirically compared; no comparison with AMAGO or other in-context RL approaches designed for long-horizon POMDPs. The strongest claims of SOTA performance are therefore not adequately supported.

Gains in some memory-intensive settings are modest or ambiguous: in Memory Maze the improvement over TrXL/RMT is small (7.64 vs 7.12-7.27) and within roughly one standard deviation; in Minigrid-Memory RATE is explicitly described as sometimes worse than TrXL or RMT, with the 'better on average' argument qualitative rather than supported by significance testing.

No code release is mentioned, and results are based on only 3-10 runs with limited seeds (Table 9), without statistical significance tests, which weakens confidence given the small margins in several tables.

The motivation around quadratic attention complexity is somewhat overstated: with only N=3-5 segments of K=20-30 steps used in the actual experiments, the sequences are short, and the paper never demonstrates RATE on sequences where the quadratic-attention limitation of DT would genuinely be prohibitive.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and well-motivated problem: extending offline RL sequence models (Decision Transformer-style) to long, partially observable trajectories where quadratic attention prevents the full trajectory from fitting in context.

The proposed RATE architecture is clearly described (Algorithms 1-2) and combines memory embeddings (RMT-style), cached hidden states (TrXL-style), and a novel cross-attention-based Memory Retention Valve that explicitly mitigates information leakage from memory during recurrent updates.

The experimental coverage is extensive and well designed: four memory-intensive environments (ViZDoom-Two-Colors, T-Maze, Memory Maze, Minigrid-Memory) plus standard Atari and MuJoCo benchmarks, with comparisons to DT, RMT, TrXL, RNN, and SSM (DMamba, MambaDM) baselines.

The ablation studies are thorough and insightful: the noise-replacement experiments (Figures 6-7) convincingly show that the model actually stores task-relevant information in memory rather than relying on spurious cues; the MRV variant ablation (Table 6) justifies the design choice; the OracleDT experiment (Table 5) provides a meaningful upper-bound estimate of what memory-based approaches can achieve.

The analysis of interpolation vs. extrapolation behavior (T-Maze and Minigrid-Memory with varying corridor/grid sizes at inference) goes beyond fixed test sets and directly probes the claimed memory capabilities.

Reproducibility materials are substantial: hyperparameters (Table 8), training details (Appendix D), evaluation protocols (Table 9), encoder configurations (Table 10), and compute/parameter budgets (Table 11) are all reported.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the core components (memory embeddings from RMT/Bulatov et al. 2022, hidden-state caching from TrXL/Dai et al. 2019, GTrXL-style gating) are established techniques combined for offline RL. The main genuinely new element is the MRV, and its mechanism is essentially a cross-attention gate; the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is conceptually new relative to applying RMT directly to DT (which is in fact one of the baselines and performs reasonably well).

The MuJoCo evaluation introduces a 'novel evaluation strategy' where each segment starts with the maximum return. It is unclear whether this strategy was also applied to the baselines (DT, TAP, etc.) or only to RATE; if not, some of the claimed MuJoCo gains may partly stem from an evaluation protocol advantage rather than the architecture, and this needs clarification.

The Atari evaluation covers only 4 games (Breakout, Qbert, SeaQuest, Pong) versus the larger suite in the DT paper, and raw (non-normalized) scores are used, complicating direct comparison; some results (e.g., Qbert 12486 vs. DT's 2215) are large jumps that would benefit from additional discussion of variance and tuning.

Some comparisons rely on scores copied from prior papers (CQL, TAP, DMamba, MambaDM) under potentially different training/tuning budgets, while all in-house baselines share the same hyperparameters 'to simplify comparison'; this may disadvantage baselines that need task-specific tuning, inflating RATE's relative advantage.

The number of runs is modest for some environments (3 runs for Memory Maze, Minigrid, Atari, MuJoCo), and no code release is explicitly promised, which weakens reproducibility despite the detailed appendices.

Claims such as the model 'compensates the effect of bias in the training data' are somewhat stronger than the evidence (a single ViZDoom dataset with a known color bias); a more cautious framing would be appropriate.

The limitations acknowledged by the authors are substantive: the effective context K_eff must be chosen a priori so key events fall within it, memory cannot be updated per-step with a sliding window, and memory capacity is uncharacterized - meaning the practical advantage over simply training RMT on DT-style sampling remains partly open.
